newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ILO chief says union freedom vital for S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: ILO chief says union freedom vital for S.Korea.

text.p: International Labour Organisation (ILO) Director-General Michel Hansenne said on Wednesday there could be no solution to South Korea's current worker unrest unless trade union freedom were respected.

Hansenne was speaking at a news conference at which he announced the United Nations' body was making a new push this year to have all its members sign up for core labour conventions including freedom of association for workers.

"It is clear that there will be no solution to the present conflict in South Korea without respect for union freedom, which is a key element in the democratic process," the Belgian ILO chief declared.

But he said he had so far received no reply to a letter on the issue he had sent last week to South Korean President Kim Young-sam, whose country joined the ILO in 1991 as it emerged from decades of military rule.

Hansenne said he could not comment on the new labour laws which have sparked the South Korean industrial crisis and which both the country's official trade union federation and the unrecognised labour confederation have denounced.
The ILO could only take a position on the legislation after discussion among the three sides that make up the organisation -- labour unions, employers and government representatives.

But Hansenne said he would have intervened with the South Korean leader on the labour freedom question even if he had not been asked to by the major global union body, the International Confederation of Free Trade unions (ICFTU).
"It seems to me evident that from the moment a country has decided to join the ILO, one of the major commitments it has taken is to respect trade union freedom," he said.

Under the new South Korean labour law, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) -- which has played a key role in the strike wave following controversial passage of the legislation -- will not be recognised until the year 2000.
The body was banned and persecuted under military governments in South Korea but Kim, himself a former dissident, has declined to move quickly to recognise it.

Arrest warrants have been issued against several leaders of the KCTU, and a Geneva-based international union body said on Wednesday its own chief had reported from Seoul that riot police appeared about to move to seize the them.

The International Metalworkers' Federation (IMWF) said its Secretary-General Marcello Malentacchi had telephoned to say that hundreds of police were surrounding the capital's Catholic cathedral and strikers expected them to break in at any time.

Earlier, the head of the labour advisory committee to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which South Korea has just joined after pledging labour freedom would be enacted, said in Seoul he and a group including Malentacchi were being harassed by police.

The group, which includes senior officials of the Brussels-based ICFTU, went to South Korea to observe the situation. The ICFTU and the IMWF have for years urged the Seoul government to recognise the KCTU.

Hansenne said the strong reaction by the global union bodies to the situation showed that as the world economy became more closely integrated no government could escape the international consequences of domestic measures.

Earlier in his news conference, he warned that governments which failed to observe basic labour standards would come under increasing pressure from trade boycotts and similar measures organised by worker bodies, consumer groups and similar non-governmental organisations in other countries.
